subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 10-month-old girl is evaluated for progressive hypotonia, poor feeding, and tachypnea. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%. Fasting during the evaluation provoked hypoglycemia (glucose 40 mg/dL) with inappropriately low urine ketones. Plasma free carnitine is markedly decreased, and plasma long-chain fatty acids are elevated.
question: Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation_correct: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is caused by loss of the sodium-dependent carnitine transporter OCTN2, so carnitine cannot enter cells and long-chain fatty acids cannot be transported into mitochondria. Cytosolic long-chain fatty acids accumulate, producing hypoketotic hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, and dilated cardiomyopathy that responds to high-dose oral carnitine.

explanation_incorrect.B: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I deficiency also causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia, but plasma carnitine is normal or elevated and cardiomyopathy is uncommon.
explanation_incorrect.C: Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency usually presents in the neonatal period with arrhythmias and accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines (C16, C18).
explanation_incorrect.D: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia with C8 acylcarnitine elevation and does not cause cardiomyopathy or low plasma carnitine.
explanation_incorrect.E: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency can cause cardiomyopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycemia, but free carnitine is normal and C14:1 acylcarnitine is elevated.

educationalObjective: Dilated cardiomyopathy with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and very low plasma free carnitine indicates systemic primary carnitine deficiency from an OCTN2 transporter defect.
